To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the five East Asian societies reviewed in the special issue have exhibited the same demographic trends and challenges to their care system, 2) the five societies have initiated different care regimes to tackle these challenges, 3) these care regimes rely on care from different sectors and 4) while the family retains its significance, its care burden is shared by other sectors.
the five Asian societies reviewed here have exhibited similar demographic challenges, which in turn have presented similar challenges to care services.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the care of the elderly, the young and the disabled are organized and delivered in East Asia.
the ways in which the five Asian societies have coped with the challenges of demographic changes and how they have responded to the demands of care.

the following: the extent to which the five East Asian societies have responded to the recent demographic challenges; the extent to which their care regimes have been reconstituted; the extent to and the ways in which care responsibilities have been redistributed; and the extent to which care responsibilities have become more or less gendered.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the care systems of these societies are in transition, with no single model being the ideal or the most effective.
care regimes are still evolving, and that their future development depends on the interplay between demographic trends and the institutional and political forces in each of these Asian countries.
there are many similarities and many differences in care regimes and responses in the five East Asian societies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the state's involvement in providing care services in these five East Asian societies is increasing.
the state has become the main provider for elderly care, while the family and market sectors are still playing a significant role in child care.
the East Asian welfare regimes are in the process of transformation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
care regimes and care arrangements are not static but are constantly being reshaped and reconfigured in response to changing needs, resources, and political forces.

care regimes and arrangements are in constant flux, responding to the changing demographic and political contexts, but also to the changing nature of family care and the state's role in care provision.
there is no 'one size fits all' care regime.
